O(log n) time and O(1) extra space, because n halves on every step and reaches 1 after about log₂ n steps.
O(n) time on average and O(n) extra space. A hash-set insert is O(1) on average, but when every key collides it is O(n), which makes the whole function O(n²) in the worst case.

copies m characters. The occasional reallocation copies the whole string, but by the argument in the second half of this page that adds only O(1) per character appended. The result holds k·m characters. Say "k·m", not "n": an interviewer listens for whether you name the variables.

c.v: The loops are written out because counting them is the exercise. In real code, 1 is
std::accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), std::int64_t{0})
, with the same O(n). A standard algorithm's cost is part of its specification, listed under "Complexity" on each cppreference page, so a call to one is counted the same way as a loop.
You pass if all five are right, including the average and worst case in 4 and both variables in 5. Missing one or two is a partial pass, and missing more is a fail.

Big-O describes how the number of steps code takes grows as its input grows, once the input is large enough that constant factors stop mattering: O(n) means the step count is at most a constant multiple of n for large n. The constant, and how fast one machine runs a step, is what Big-O leaves out.
Extra space
is the same idea applied to memory: everything code allocates beyond its input, including every level of a recursion's stack.

The problem it solves is comparing two pieces of code without running either, without being fooled by whichever is faster on today's input. A loop over a list is fast for ten elements whatever its growth rate, and slow for a million only if the rate is bad, so reasoning about growth, not one timing, tells you which code is still running once the input is large. Two loops that look alike, one nested and one where the inner loop halves each time, cost O(n²) and O(n): counting the steps, not the shape, tells them apart.

You get Big-O by counting: add the costs of steps that run one after another and keep the largest term, multiply the costs of nested loops, and count a loop whose variable halves or doubles each time as O(log n) rather than O(n). With two independent input sizes, keep both, since O(n + m) and O(n·m) differ.
Amortised
cost extends the same counting across a sequence of calls:
push_back

occasionally costs O(n), when it must grow and move every element, but each growth doubles the capacity, so the moves to reach n elements never exceed twice n, and the cost per push, averaged over the sequence, is O(1).

What matters once you have a rate is not blurring amortised, average and worst case together. An amortised bound holds for every sequence whatever the input; an average is taken over inputs and can still be bad for one, the way a hash-table lookup is O(1) on average but O(n) when every key lands in one bucket. Naming which of the three you mean, and naming your variables instead of one n, is what most answers leave out.

That is why an interviewer asks for it first: a growth rate tells them, without running your code, whether it finishes at the size their system sees, and every later page on this track expects it of your solution.

subs.title: Big-O for loops, nested loops, halving and extra storage

c.v: Both loops below look like a loop inside a loop. Count their steps:

The first makes n(n−1)/2 = 523,776 steps for n = 1024, which is O(n²). The second makes 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 512 = 1023 steps, which is O(n): its outer loop runs only log₂ n times, and the inner counts add up to less than 2n. You get Big-O by counting what the code does, not by looking at how its loops are nested. Kirsh and Segoli Schubert's Back to Basics talk on complexity (CppCon 2021) quizzes its audience with code of this kind.

Big-O describes how the number of steps grows as the input grows, ignoring constant factors: O(n) means at most a constant times n once n is large enough. To get it from code, add the costs of code that runs one after the other and keep the largest term, multiply the costs of nested loops, and count a loop whose variable halves or doubles as log n. When the input has two sizes, keep both. O(n + m) and O(n·m) are different answers, and collapsing them into n loses what an interviewer is asking for.
Space works the same way.
Extra space

is the memory you use beyond the input: new containers, the output if you build it, and the recursion stack, where every level of depth counts. In an interview, give both time and extra space and name the variables, for example "O(n log n) time and O(n) extra space, where n is the number of intervals".

This program pushes 20 elements into an empty vector and prints a line each time the capacity changes. Each
Counted
element carries the number of times it has been moved: the move constructor gives the new element the old count plus one.

blocks.text:
size  1 -> capacity 1
size  2 -> capacity 2
size  3 -> capacity 4
size  5 -> capacity 8
size  9 -> capacity 16
size 17 -> capacity 32
20 pushes made 31 moves; element 1 moved 5 times, element 20 0 times

c.v: Six of the 20 pushes found the vector full. Each of them allocated a new block, twice the old capacity once there was one, moved every element across and freed the old block. They moved 0, 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 elements. The other 14 pushes moved nothing. Element 1 went through five of those moves, and element 20 arrived after the last one.

So a single push can cost O(n), but a sequence of pushes can't average out that badly. Because the capacity doubles, the moves needed to reach n elements add up to less than 2n, and the cost per push over the whole sequence is constant. That is what
amortised O(1)
means, and it is what cppreference's page on
push_back
gives as its complexity. The growth factor is the library's choice. GCC's libstdc++ doubles the capacity: its
_M_check_len
asks for the old size plus the larger of the old size and the number of new elements. Microsoft's library grows it by 1.5, as its
_Calculate_growth
in the
microsoft/STL sources
shows, which is still amortised O(1), with more reallocations.
Amortised cost is often confused with average cost. An amortised bound holds for every sequence of operations, whatever the input. An average is taken over inputs.
std::unordered_map::find
is O(1) on average, but when every key lands in the same bucket it is O(n), and no argument about sequences changes that.
If you know the final size,
reserve(n)
allocates once and the moves disappear, which is Core Guidelines
Per.14

, "minimize the number of allocations and deallocations". Growth also has a cost that matters more than time: it invalidates every pointer, reference and iterator into the vector. The topic on iterators and invalidation covers the bugs this causes.
Take 15 minutes.

c.v: Solution
With
reserve(20)
, the program prints no capacity lines, and the last line reads
20 pushes made 0 moves; element 1 moved 0 times, element 20 0 times
. The capacity is already 20 when
last
is read, and it never changes inside the loop.

A doubling vector reallocates about 20 times on the way to a million elements, because 2²⁰ is about 10⁶. Counting capacity changes in libstdc++ gives 21: the first allocation, then 20 reallocations, ending at a capacity of 2²⁰ = 1,048,576.
Without
noexcept
, the vector copies instead of moving. When it grows,
std::vector

promises that a push which throws leaves the vector as it was: the strong exception guarantee. If a move threw halfway through, some elements would already have left the old block, and that promise would be broken. So the vector moves elements only when the move constructor can't throw, or when the type can't be copied at all, which is the rule
std::move_if_noexcept
expresses, and copies them otherwise. That is the practical reason to mark move constructors
noexcept
, and Arthur O'Dwyer calls the slow path the
vector pessimization
